q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE reason for the decline of death rates after 1950.
parts.b: Explain ONE way in which falling death rates affected population growth in developing countries, using the historian's interpretation in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which demographic patterns in developed countries differed from those in developing countries in the late twentieth century.

sample_answers.a: The spread of antibiotics, vaccines, and insecticides (such as DDT against malaria), along with improved sanitation and nutrition, drastically reduced deaths from infectious disease, especially among infants and children.
sample_answers.b: According to the passage, when death rates fell rapidly but birth rates remained high, populations exploded: more children survived to adulthood and had children of their own, producing the fastest population growth in human history.
sample_answers.c: Developed countries completed the demographic transition — birth rates fell alongside death rates as urbanization, education, and contraception spread — leading to aging populations and even population decline, while developing countries still had youthful, rapidly growing populations.

q1.stimulus:
Historians describe the twentieth century's population explosion as the result of death control without birth control. After 1950, the transfer of medical and public-health technologies — antibiotics, vaccines, DDT, sanitary engineering — caused death rates to plummet across Asia, Africa, and Latin America within a single generation. But birth rates, sustained by cultural norms, the economic value of children, and limited access to contraception, remained high for decades. The result was unprecedented: world population doubled from 2.5 billion in 1950 to 5 billion by 1987, with most growth in the poorest countries. By century's end, however, a new pattern emerged: as education (especially for women), urbanization, and family planning spread, birth rates fell sharply even in developing regions, and demographers began projecting an eventual stabilization of world population.
—Historian's account of demographic change in the period c. 1900–present

q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE claim Malthus makes about population growth.
parts.b: Describe ONE way in which twentieth-century developments challenged Malthus's predictions.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why Malthus's ideas remained influential despite these developments.

sample_answers.a: Malthus claims that population, when unchecked, grows geometrically (1, 2, 4, 8...) while food production grows only arithmetically (1, 2, 3, 4...), so population will inevitably outstrip resources unless checked by misery or vice.
sample_answers.b: The Green Revolution, synthetic fertilizers, and mechanized agriculture multiplied food production far faster than Malthus thought possible, while contraception allowed populations to limit births voluntarily — so food supply kept pace with (and often outran) population growth.
sample_answers.c: Malthus captured a real insight — that finite resources constrain infinite growth — which seemed validated by famines, environmental crises, and fears of overpopulation; his framework offered a simple, powerful way to think about scarcity.

q2.stimulus:
I think I may fairly make two postulata. First, That food is necessary to the existence of man. Secondly, That the passion between the sexes is necessary and will remain nearly in its present state. Assuming then my postulata as granted, I say, that the power of population is indefinitely greater than the power in the earth to produce subsistence for man. Population, when unchecked, increases in a geometrical ratio. Subsistence increases only in an arithmetical ratio.
—Thomas Malthus, An Essay on the Principle of Population, 1798

q3.directions: Use the chart below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE trend shown in the chart of world population.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of the rapid population growth shown in the chart after 1950.
parts.c: Explain ONE consequence of the population trend shown in the chart for the twenty-first century.

sample_answers.a: The chart shows world population growing slowly for most of human history, then exploding upward after 1900 — and especially after 1950 — from about 2.5 billion to 8 billion in just over seventy years.
sample_answers.b: Falling death rates from modern medicine and public health (vaccines, antibiotics, sanitation) meant far more children survived and adults lived longer, while birth rates stayed high, producing a surge of net population growth.
sample_answers.c: The sheer scale of humanity — 8 billion and rising — intensifies pressure on food, water, energy, and the climate, making sustainable development one of the century's central challenges even as growth rates slow.

q3.stimulus: The chart shows the growth of world human population over time, from the distant past to the present. For most of history the curve rises very gradually, but from the eighteenth century it begins to climb steeply, and after 1950 it shoots almost vertically upward — the demographic explosion that took world population from about 2.5 billion in 1950 to 8 billion today.
